statement: On the S&P scale the investment-grade ratings run from AAA to BBB, and for them the marginal probability of default tends to rise with time in the first few years after the rating is assigned.
explanation: Investment-grade issuers start creditworthy, and the longer the period the greater the chance that their financial health declines, so the year-by-year PD tends to rise. GARP's example is the A grade: 0.05%, 0.08%, 0.09% and 0.11% in successive years.
originalText: AAA to BBB; the marginal PD tends to rise with time because the issuer starts creditworthy and the longer the period, the greater the chance that its financial health declines.

statement: For investment-grade issuers (AAA to BBB), the marginal probability of default tends to fall with time in the first few years after the rating is assigned.
explanation: For investment-grade issuers the marginal PD tends to rise with time. A falling profile belongs to poorly rated issuers, where the survivors of the first year or two are healthier.
originalText: AAA to BBB; the marginal PD falls with time because the next year or two are critical and the survivors are healthier.
correction: For investment-grade issuers (AAA to BBB), the marginal probability of default tends to rise with time in the first few years after the rating is assigned.

statement: The investment-grade range on the S&P scale runs from AAA to BB.
explanation: On the S&P scale AAA, AA, A and BBB are investment grade; BB and below are non-investment grade.
originalText: AAA to BB; the marginal PD is constant because rating agencies rate through the cycle.
correction: The investment-grade range on the S&P scale runs from AAA to BBB.

statement: The conditional probability of default of CCC/C issuers falls with time, which shows that an issuer that survives the first year or two is genuinely less likely to default and not merely one of a shrinking pool.
explanation: The conditional PD divides each year's defaults by the issuers still alive, so a shrinking pool cannot by itself make it fall. Its fall for CCC/C issuers (28.30% to 13.99%, 8.25%, 5.20% and 4.14%) reflects genuinely healthier survivors.
originalText: The manager is wrong: the conditional PD, which already removes the effect of the shrinking pool, also falls, so a CCC/C issuer that survives the first year or two is genuinely less likely to default.

statement: With a constant hazard rate, the conditional probability of default falls from year to year.
explanation: With a constant hazard rate the conditional PD is the same every year (the memoryless property); it is the unconditional PD that falls slowly.
originalText: The manager is right: with a constant hazard rate the conditional PD would fall in exactly this way.
correction: With a constant hazard rate, the conditional probability of default is constant from year to year.

statement: In agency default tables, the inverse relationship between rating and cumulative default rate holds across the scale as a whole but not strictly between the top two grades, where AAA can show a higher cumulative default rate than AA at some horizons.
explanation: In GARP's Table 9.1 AAA's cumulative default rate is above AA's at 5 and 7 years and equal at 10 years, although every lower grade is above the grade before it. Between the top two grades defaults are so rare that the ordering is not strict.
originalText: The sentence fails: AAA’s rate is above AA’s at 5 and 7 years and equal at 10 years. The inverse relationship holds across the scale as a whole but not strictly between the top two grades.

statement: The cumulative default rate of a given rating falls as the horizon lengthens.
explanation: A cumulative default rate cannot fall as the horizon lengthens, because it counts all defaults up to that date; for AAA it rises from 0.34% at 5 years to 0.90% at 15 years.
originalText: The sentence fails because AAA cumulative default rates fall at longer horizons.
correction: The cumulative default rate of a given rating rises as the horizon lengthens.

statement: The inverse relationship between rating and probability of default compares borrowers at the same horizon, and because cumulative default probabilities rise with the horizon, a long-dated loan to a better-rated borrower can have a higher lifetime default probability than a short-dated loan to a worse-rated one.
explanation: In GARP Table 9.1 the 15-year cumulative default rate of a BBB borrower (4.54%) exceeds the one-year rate of a B borrower (3.34%). The rating ranks borrowers at a fixed horizon, and a longer horizon gives a borrower time to deteriorate.
originalText: The BBB loan has the higher probability of default over its life (4.54% against 3.34%): the inverse relationship between rating and PD compares borrowers at the same horizon, and cumulative PDs rise with the horizon.

statement: A lower-rated borrower always has a higher cumulative probability of default than a better-rated borrower, whatever the horizons being compared.
explanation: The ranking by rating holds only when the horizon is the same. Cumulative default probabilities rise with the horizon, so a long-dated exposure to a better-rated borrower can carry a higher lifetime PD than a short-dated exposure to a worse-rated one.
originalText: The B loan has the higher probability of default, because a lower rating means a higher probability of default whatever the horizon.

statement: By the usual convention, the recovery rate on a defaulted bond is the price at which the bond trades about one month after default, expressed as a percentage of its principal amount.
explanation: A market price shortly after default gives a timely, observable number for every defaulted bond. Loss given default is then one minus the recovery rate.
originalText: As the price at which the bond trades about one month after default, as a percentage of its principal amount.

statement: By the usual convention, the recovery rate on a defaulted bond is the amount finally paid to bondholders at the end of the bankruptcy process, as a percentage of the bond's market price just before default.
explanation: The recovery rate is read from the bond's market price about one month after default and is expressed as a percentage of principal, not of the pre-default price and not after the bankruptcy process ends.
originalText: As the amount finally paid to bondholders at the end of the bankruptcy process, as a percentage of the bond’s market price just before default.

statement: By the usual convention, the recovery rate on a defaulted bond is the bond's price immediately before default, as a percentage of its principal amount.
explanation: A pre-default price reflects the market's view before the event, not what is recovered. The recovery rate is taken from the price about one month after default.
originalText: As the bond’s price immediately before default, as a percentage of its principal amount.

statement: In Moody's average recovery data, bonds with a claim on collateral recover more than unsecured bonds and recovery broadly falls with seniority, although subordinated bonds have recovered slightly more on average than senior subordinated bonds.
explanation: Moody's issuer-weighted averages for 1983 to 2021 are 54.6% for first lien, 44.3% for second lien and 38.0% for senior unsecured. Further down, senior subordinated bonds recovered 31.0% against 32.1% for subordinated, a small reversal.
originalText: Bonds with a claim on collateral recover more on average than unsecured bonds, and recovery broadly falls with seniority, although subordinated bonds recovered slightly more on average than senior subordinated bonds.

statement: Second lien bonds recover more on average than first lien bonds.
explanation: First lien bonds have the first claim on collateral and recover more on average (54.6% against 44.3% in Moody's 1983 to 2021 data).
originalText: Second lien bonds recover more on average than first lien bonds, because they also have a claim on collateral.
correction: Second lien bonds recover less on average than first lien bonds.

statement: Average recovery rates fall strictly with each step down in seniority, so subordinated bonds always recover less than senior subordinated bonds.
explanation: Recovery broadly falls with seniority but not strictly: in Moody's 1983 to 2021 averages subordinated bonds (32.1%) recovered slightly more than senior subordinated bonds (31.0%).
originalText: Recovery falls strictly with each step down in seniority, so subordinated bonds always recover less than senior subordinated bonds.

statement: Rising mortgage default rates lead to more foreclosures, more houses offered for sale and falling house prices, which reduce recovery rates.
explanation: The lender recovers what the collateral fetches. The extra supply of foreclosed houses pushes prices down, so recovery rates on defaulted mortgages fall: the economy that causes defaults also lowers what defaulted assets are worth.
originalText: Rising default rates led to more foreclosures, more houses offered for sale and falling house prices, which reduced recovery rates.

statement: Rising mortgage default rates lead lenders to hold foreclosed houses off the market, which keeps house prices and recovery rates stable.
explanation: Foreclosed houses were offered for sale, house prices fell and recovery rates dropped; defaults and recoveries are negatively related.
originalText: Rising default rates led lenders to hold foreclosed houses off the market, which kept house prices and recovery rates stable.

statement: Assigning a fixed recovery rate to every defaulted loan understates losses in high-default years, so the tail of the simulated loss distribution, and any credit VaR read from it, is too thin.
explanation: Recovery rates fall when default rates are high, so a fixed rate near the long-run average is too high exactly in the worst years. Expected loss can look about right while the tail is wrong.
originalText: Losses in high-default years are understated, so the tail of the loss distribution, and any credit VaR read from it, is too thin: in practice those years also bring lower recoveries.

statement: Recovery rates tend to rise in years when many firms default.
explanation: Default rates and recovery rates are negatively related: in high-default years recoveries are low, as low as about 30%, as collateral values and the buyers for defaulted assets dry up.
originalText: Losses in high-default years are overstated, because recoveries rise when many firms default and collateral markets deepen.
correction: Recovery rates tend to fall in years when many firms default.

statement: Once seniority is fixed, recovery rates are unrelated to default rates.
explanation: Seniority does not remove the cyclical link: the average recovery rate in a year moves inversely with the default rate.
originalText: The tail is unaffected, because once seniority is fixed, recovery rates are unrelated to default rates.

statement: For CCC/C bonds, the hazard rate calculated from historical default probabilities exceeds the hazard rate implied by credit spreads.
explanation: The spread-implied hazard rate is above the historical one for every rating, including CCC/C (18.395% against 10.118% in GARP Table 9.5). Investors earn an excess return over historical default experience.
originalText: For CCC/C bonds the historical hazard rate exceeds the spread-implied one, so investors in the lowest grade are under-compensated.
correction: For CCC/C bonds, the hazard rate calculated from historical default probabilities is below the hazard rate implied by credit spreads.

statement: The excess of the spread-implied hazard rate over the historical hazard rate falls as credit quality declines.
explanation: The excess rises as credit quality declines (from about 1.0 percentage point for A to about 8.3 for CCC/C), and illiquidity adds to it rather than explaining a fall.
originalText: The excess falls as credit quality declines, because low-quality bonds are more liquid.
correction: The excess of the spread-implied hazard rate over the historical hazard rate rises as credit quality declines.

statement: The main reason default probabilities implied by credit spreads are much higher than those calculated from historical data is that bonds do not default independently, so bondholders bear systematic risk that cannot be diversified away and earn an excess return for it.
explanation: Default rates swing from year to year (0.15% in 1981 to 4.19% in 2009), so default risk is partly systematic. Illiquidity explains only a small part of the gap.
originalText: Bonds do not default independently of each other, so bondholders bear systematic risk that cannot be diversified away and earn an excess return for it.

statement: Bond illiquidity and the liquidity premium explain most of the gap between default probabilities implied by credit spreads and those calculated from historical data.
explanation: Illiquidity explains only a small part of the gap (perhaps 25 bp in normal markets). The main reason is that default risk is partly systematic and non-diversifiable, so bondholders earn an excess return.
originalText: Corporate bonds are relatively illiquid, and the liquidity premium explains most of the gap.

statement: Converting Merton default probabilities into real-world default probabilities through a monotonic transformation assumes that the rankings of risk-neutral, real-world and Merton default probabilities are all the same.
explanation: A monotonic transformation changes levels but preserves the order of firms, so the mapping works only if all three measures rank firms identically.
originalText: The rankings of risk-neutral default probabilities, real-world default probabilities and Merton default probabilities are all the same.

statement: Risk-neutral and real-world default probabilities are equal in level, so no adjustment for risk premiums is needed.
explanation: Risk-neutral default probabilities are higher than real-world ones, because they include risk premiums. That difference in level is exactly what the calibration adjusts.
originalText: The levels of risk-neutral and real-world default probabilities are equal, so no adjustment for risk premiums is needed.

statement: The Merton default probability $N(-d_2)$, calculated from an option pricing model, is already a real-world default probability.
explanation: In theory $N(-d_2)$ is a risk-neutral default probability because it comes from an option pricing model, so it must be mapped to real-world probabilities.
originalText: Merton default probabilities are already real-world probabilities, so the transformation only corrects estimation error.

statement: Real-world default probabilities exceed risk-neutral default probabilities.
explanation: Real-world default probabilities are lower than risk-neutral ones, which include a risk premium.
originalText: Real-world default probabilities exceed risk-neutral ones, so the transformation must raise every Merton probability.
correction: Real-world default probabilities are lower than risk-neutral default probabilities.

statement: The Moody's KMV model maps the distance to default to a probability through an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies, and sets the default point at short-term debt plus half of long-term debt.
explanation: Plain Merton reads the probability off the normal distribution, $N(-d_2)$. KMV's empirical mapping and its default point, which better approximates the firm's actual obligations, both aim at more realistic real-world levels.
originalText: KMV maps the distance to default to a probability through an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies, and sets the default point at short-term debt plus half of long-term debt.

statement: The Moody's KMV model reads the default probability off the standard normal distribution, $N(-\text{DD})$, and uses total debt as the default point.
explanation: That describes a plain Merton approach. KMV uses an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies and sets the default point at short-term debt plus half of long-term debt.
originalText: KMV reads the probability off the standard normal distribution, $N (-\text{DD})$, but uses total debt as the default point.

statement: The Moody's KMV model replaces the equity-based distance to default with the borrower's agency rating and a rating transition matrix.
explanation: Rating transition matrices belong to CreditMetrics. KMV is built on the equity-based distance to default, which it maps to an empirical default frequency.
originalText: KMV replaces the equity-based distance to default with the borrower’s agency rating and a rating transition matrix.

statement: The Moody's KMV model uses the book value of equity rather than its market value.
explanation: KMV uses the market value of equity, which is why its estimates respond quickly to market information.
originalText: KMV uses the book value of equity rather than its market value, which makes its probabilities more stable.
correction: The Moody's KMV model uses the market value of equity rather than its book value.

changes.from: book value of equity rather than its market value
changes.to: market value of equity rather than its book value

statement: Default probabilities from Moody's KMV and Kamakura are based on equity prices and other market variables, do not target stability and respond more quickly to market information than agency ratings do.
explanation: Ratings are revised infrequently and aim for stability, whereas the market-based estimates move with market information. That makes them useful early-warning signals for borrowers with traded equity.
originalText: Sensible for the listed borrowers: the estimates are based on equity prices, do not target stability and respond more quickly to market information than ratings; they cannot be produced for borrowers without traded equity.

statement: Like agency ratings, the default probability estimates of Moody's KMV and Kamakura aim for stability and avoid reversals, so they react slowly.
explanation: Stability is an objective of agency ratings, not of the market-based models, whose estimates respond quickly to market information.
originalText: Not sensible: like agency ratings, these estimates aim for stability and avoid reversals, so they react slowly.

statement: The default probability models of Moody's KMV and Kamakura need only accounting data.
explanation: These models rely on equity prices and other market variables, so they cannot simply be applied to borrowers without market prices.
originalText: Sensible for every borrower, including the private firms, because the models need only accounting data.

statement: In Credit Risk Plus, making the default rate uncertain while keeping the expected number of defaults unchanged raises the 99.9th percentile of the number of defaults.
explanation: With the mean fixed at 4, raising the default-rate volatility from 0 to 10 lifts the 99.9th percentile of the number of defaults from 11 to 98 (GARP Table 10.4). Default-rate uncertainty is how Credit Risk Plus creates default correlation and fat tails.
originalText: In Credit Risk Plus, making the default rate uncertain while keeping the expected number of defaults unchanged raises the 99.9th percentile of the number of defaults.

statement: Credit Risk Plus estimates each obligor's default probability from its capital structure and asset volatility.
explanation: Credit Risk Plus is an actuarial default-count model that does not use the capital structure. Estimating default probabilities from capital structure and asset volatility is the KMV approach.
originalText: Credit Risk Plus estimates each obligor’s default probability from its capital structure and asset volatility.

statement: Vasicek's model captures losses from both downgrades and defaults.
explanation: Vasicek's model counts defaults only. Capturing losses from downgrades as well as defaults is a feature of CreditMetrics.
originalText: Vasicek’s model captures losses from both downgrades and defaults, which is why regulators use it for IRB capital.

statement: Vasicek's Gaussian copula model generates strong tail dependence between defaults.
explanation: The Gaussian copula incorporates very little tail dependence; a different copula is needed to add it.
originalText: Because it uses a Gaussian copula, Vasicek’s model generates strong tail dependence between defaults.
correction: Vasicek's Gaussian copula model generates very little tail dependence between defaults.

statement: Credit Risk Plus recognises no credit loss on a loan until it defaults, and it generates default correlation through uncertainty in a default rate shared by all obligors.
explanation: Credit Risk Plus and Vasicek recognise loss only on default, whereas CreditMetrics books a revaluation loss at each downgrade. Credit Risk Plus's correlation comes from the common uncertain default rate.
originalText: Credit Risk Plus recognises no loss until the default in year 3, and it generates default correlation through uncertainty in the default rate shared by all obligors.

statement: CreditMetrics recognises no credit loss on a loan until it defaults.
explanation: CreditMetrics books a revaluation loss at each downgrade as it happens, not only at default.
originalText: CreditMetrics recognises no loss until the default in year 3, and it generates default correlation by making the expected number of defaults gamma-distributed.

statement: CreditMetrics treats the rating changes of different obligors as independent of each other.
explanation: CreditMetrics correlates the rating changes of different obligors through a Gaussian copula, using equity-return correlations.
originalText: CreditMetrics recognises revaluation losses in years 1, 2 and 3, but it treats the rating changes of different obligors as independent.

statement: Vasicek's model recognises revaluation losses from downgrades through a transition matrix.
explanation: Vasicek's model has no transition matrix: it counts defaults only and correlates them with a one-factor Gaussian copula.
originalText: Vasicek’s model recognises revaluation losses in years 1 and 2 through a transition matrix, and it correlates defaults through a gamma-distributed default rate.

statement: Including credit spread risk can raise the short-horizon credit VaR of a bond portfolio above that of a default-only model, because bond values fall when spreads widen or ratings fall even when no issuer defaults.
explanation: If default is very unlikely over the horizon, the 99th percentile of a default-only loss is close to zero. Spread widening and downgrades cause losses on many days without any default, and these populate the tail.
originalText: The VaR would rise, because bond values fall when spreads widen or ratings fall, so losses appear at the 99th percentile even though no issuer defaults.

statement: Credit VaR by definition covers only losses from default, so spread changes, which are a market risk, are excluded from it.
explanation: Credit VaR models can also include losses from downgrades and credit spread changes. Leaving them out does not make them disappear.
originalText: The VaR would be unchanged, because spread changes are a market risk and credit VaR covers default losses only by definition.

statement: In Malz's single-factor model, a higher common beta makes both very few and very many defaults more likely in a large homogeneous loan book, so Credit VaR rises with beta, and for any beta above zero it stays positive however many loans are added.
explanation: A higher beta makes the conditional default probability more sensitive to the market factor, widening the loss distribution. Granularity removes only the idiosyncratic part of the risk, not the common factor.
originalText: A higher $\beta$ makes both very few and very many defaults more likely, so the 99% Credit VaR rises; for any $\beta> 0$ it stays positive however many loans are added.

statement: In the single-factor model, a higher common beta raises the expected loss rate of a homogeneous loan book above the individual default probability.
explanation: The expected loss rate equals the default probability for every beta. Correlation reshapes the distribution of losses around that mean without changing it.
originalText: A higher $\beta$ raises the book’s expected loss rate above 2%, which is why Credit VaR rises with $\beta$.

statement: In the single-factor model, as beta approaches 1 the loss rate of a granular book converges to the default probability in every state of the economy, so Credit VaR falls towards zero.
explanation: The loss rate converges to the default probability as beta approaches 0. As beta approaches 1 the loss rate is either 0 or 100%, so Credit VaR rises.
originalText: As $\beta$ approaches 1, the loss rate converges to 2% in every state of the economy, so Credit VaR falls towards zero.

statement: Once a loan book is granular, the market factor no longer moves its loss rate, so Credit VaR is close to zero whatever the value of beta.
explanation: Granularity removes only the idiosyncratic part of the risk. The loss rate still moves with the market factor whenever beta is positive, so Credit VaR stays positive.
originalText: Once the book is this granular the market factor no longer moves the loss rate, so Credit VaR is close to zero whatever the value of $\beta$.

statement: Splitting one loan to a single obligor into many smaller loans to the same obligor changes nothing in substance: the loans default together, so the book still behaves as one credit and its Credit VaR is unchanged.
explanation: Debts of the same obligor are equivalent to one large position, with a default correlation of 1. The loss is the full amount with the same probability before and after the split.
originalText: Nothing has changed in substance: the 50 loans default together, so the book still behaves as a single credit and its Credit VaR is unchanged.

statement: Splitting one loan into many smaller loans to the same obligor makes the book granular, so its Credit VaR falls.
explanation: Granularity requires many separate obligors. Loans to the same obligor all default together, so the number of defaults is not binomial and Credit VaR does not fall.
originalText: The book is now granular: with 50 positions the number of defaults is binomial, so the 99% Credit VaR falls.

statement: Making a loan book more granular lowers its Credit VaR, but with a positive default correlation it cannot bring Credit VaR to zero, because losses on the granular book still move with the common factor.
explanation: In the single-factor model the loss rate of a granular book converges to the conditional default probability, which still depends on the common factor. Only independent positions would drive Credit VaR to zero.
originalText: The move lowers Credit VaR, but with a positive default correlation it cannot bring Credit VaR to zero, because losses on the granular book still move with the common factor.

statement: The proportional reduction in Credit VaR from greater granularity is largest when the default probability of the loans is low.
explanation: Per Malz, the convergence is more drastic with a high default probability, and it is harder to reduce Credit VaR by making a portfolio more granular when the default probability is low.
originalText: The move lowers Credit VaR, and the proportional reduction from granularity is largest when the default probability of the loans is low.
correction: The proportional reduction in Credit VaR from greater granularity is largest when the default probability of the loans is high.

statement: With enough borrowers, granularity drives Credit VaR to zero whatever the default correlation.
explanation: Credit VaR goes to zero only for a very large number of independent positions. With a positive default correlation the common factor remains and Credit VaR stays positive.
originalText: The move lowers Credit VaR and, with enough borrowers, drives it to zero whatever the default correlation, because the loss rate converges to the default probability.

statement: Greater granularity lowers a loan portfolio's expected loss, which is why its Credit VaR falls.
explanation: Granularity does not change the expected loss, which stays equal to the default probability times the portfolio value. It reduces the dispersion and the extreme quantiles of loss.
originalText: The move lowers Credit VaR, because spreading the book across more borrowers lowers the portfolio’s expected loss, and the expected loss is subtracted from the loss quantile.

statement: In the Gaussian copula model for time to default, the copula correlation is the correlation between the transformed standard normal variables $x_i = N^{-1}[Q_i(t_i)]$, not between the default times themselves.
explanation: The copula maps each time to default $t_i$ into a standard normal $x_i$ and assumes the $x_i$ are multivariate normal. The correlation between $x_i$ and $x_j$ is called the copula correlation, and the default correlation it implies is much lower.
originalText: It is the correlation between the transformed standard normal variables $x_{i} = N^{-1}[Q_{i}(t_{i})]$; the default correlation it implies over five years is much lower, below 0.1.

statement: In the Gaussian copula model, the copula correlation is the correlation between the companies' times to default, because the copula is applied directly to the default times.
explanation: The copula is applied to the transformed variables $x_i$, precisely because times to default are not normally distributed.
originalText: It is the correlation between the two companies’ times to default, because the copula is applied directly to the default times.

statement: In the Gaussian copula model, the copula correlation is the correlation between the default indicators of two companies over the horizon, so it can be used directly in the default correlation formula.
explanation: The copula correlation is the correlation of transformed normal variables. The default correlation it implies over a horizon is a different and much lower number.
originalText: It is the correlation between the default indicators of any two companies over the five years, so it can be used directly in the default correlation formula.

statement: In a Gaussian copula model, raising the copula correlation raises each company's probability of default over a given horizon.
explanation: The copula leaves each company's marginal default probability untouched. A higher correlation changes how defaults cluster, not how likely each one is.
originalText: Raising it from 0.2 to 0.4 would raise each company’s five-year default probability above 15%, because defaults would cluster.

statement: A physically settled European payer swaption that is not exercised because the underlying swap is out of the money on the exercise date ceases to exist on that path, whereas an otherwise identical forward-starting swap still starts and can have positive exposure.
explanation: A forward swap is an obligation, so it starts regardless of its value. A rational holder does not exercise an out-of-the-money option, so the swaption has no exposure afterwards.
originalText: Only the forward swap has exposure: the swaption was not exercised when the swap was out of the money, so it no longer exists on this path.

statement: A forward-starting swap is cancelled if it is out of the money on its start date.
explanation: A forward-starting swap is an obligation and is not cancelled when it is out of the money; the right to walk away belongs to the option holder.
originalText: Only the swaption has exposure: the forward-starting swap is cancelled when it is out of the money on the exercise date.

statement: If the exercise decision is based on the base value of the underlying swap, the simulated valuation paths are the same for cash- and physically settled swaptions, and exposure can be computed directly from the simulated future values.
explanation: Basing exercise on the base value avoids a link between exposure and the exercise decision, so no recursion is needed.
originalText: If the exercise decision is based on the base value of the underlying swap, the simulated valuation paths are the same for cash- and physically settled swaptions, and exposure can be computed directly from the simulated future values.

statement: Exercise decisions can be ignored when simulating exposure, as they are in 10-day VaR models, because they occur only on discrete dates.
explanation: Only the short horizon of a 10-day VaR allows exercise to be ignored. Exposure is defined over many horizons, so exercise decisions, cash flows and margin must be carried forward.
originalText: Exercise decisions can be ignored when simulating exposure, as they are in 10-day VaR models, because they occur only on discrete dates.

statement: If the exercise decision is based on the actual value including xVA, exposure becomes independent of the exercise boundary and the recursion in the calculation disappears.
explanation: Using the actual value makes exposure and the exercise decision depend on each other, which creates the recursion rather than removing it.
originalText: If the exercise decision is based on the actual value including xVA, exposure becomes independent of the exercise boundary, which removes any recursion from the calculation.

statement: For a Bermudan swaption with several exercise dates, only the first exercise decision needs to be modelled, because later decisions are implied by it.
explanation: Where multiple exercise decisions are taken, all possible combinations of them must be considered.
originalText: For a Bermudan swaption with several exercise dates, only the first exercise decision needs to be modelled, because later decisions are implied by it.

statement: Average EPE is the time-weighted average of the EPE profile, often called the loan equivalent, while maximum PFE is the peak of the PFE profile over the life of the portfolio.
explanation: Average EPE weights the EPE profile by the time intervals and gives a single number. Maximum PFE is the highest point of the PFE profile.
originalText: Average EPE is the time-weighted average of the EPE profile, often called the loan equivalent, while maximum PFE is the peak of the PFE profile over the life of the portfolio.

statement: Expected future value and expected positive exposure are both additive across transactions, so the EPE of a netting set equals the sum of the EPEs of its trades.
explanation: Only expected future value is additive. EPE is sub-additive because $\max(\sum v_i, 0) \le \sum \max(v_i, 0)$, and that gap is the netting benefit.
originalText: Expected future value and expected positive exposure are both additive across transactions, so the EPE of a netting set equals the sum of the EPEs of its trades.

statement: Expected negative exposure is the driver of the credit value adjustment that a bank charges its counterparty.
explanation: Expected positive exposure drives CVA. Expected negative exposure is the exposure from the counterparty's point of view and drives the bank's own DVA.
originalText: Expected negative exposure is the exposure seen from the counterparty’s point of view, so it drives the credit value adjustment the bank charges that counterparty.
correction: Expected positive exposure is the driver of the credit value adjustment that a bank charges its counterparty.

statement: Doubling the volatility of future value, with expected future value unchanged, lowers expected positive exposure.
explanation: Exposure is option-like, so higher volatility raises EPE while the expected future value is unchanged.
originalText: Doubling the volatility of future value leaves the expected future value unchanged but lowers expected positive exposure, because more scenarios end below zero.
correction: Doubling the volatility of future value, with expected future value unchanged, raises expected positive exposure.

statement: A new trade whose value is highly positively correlated with an existing netting set can still have an incremental EPE well below its standalone EPE when the netting set is deep out of the money, because the netting set is unlikely to turn positive unless the market moves a long way.
explanation: Aggregation benefits come from relative moneyness as well as from structural correlation. A deeply negative portfolio absorbs most of the new trade's positive value.
originalText: Although the values are highly correlated, the netting set is unlikely to have positive value unless rates rise a long way, so the incremental EPE will be well below the new trade’s standalone EPE.

statement: Because a new trade is highly positively correlated with the existing trades in a netting set, aggregation gives no benefit and its incremental EPE equals its standalone EPE.
explanation: Positive correlation of values does not mean the positive parts move together: if the portfolio is deeply negative, it offsets much of the new trade's positive exposure.
originalText: Because the new trade is highly positively correlated with the existing swaps, aggregation gives no benefit and the incremental EPE equals the new trade’s standalone EPE.

statement: Because expected future value is additive, the EPE of a netting set equals the standalone EPE of a new trade plus the existing portfolio's expected future value.
explanation: EFV is additive but EPE is not, so an EPE cannot be found by adding an EFV to a standalone EPE.
originalText: Because EFV is additive and the portfolio’s EFV is negative, the netting set’s EPE equals the new trade’s standalone EPE plus the portfolio’s EFV.

statement: An out-of-the-money portfolio raises the incremental exposure of any new trade added to its netting set.
explanation: An out-of-the-money portfolio dampens the incremental exposure of a new trade, because it must recover before the netting set has positive value.
originalText: An out-of-the-money portfolio raises the incremental exposure of any new trade, because the bank already owes the client money.

statement: A positive portfolio value is at risk if the counterparty defaults and is also an asset that must be funded while the counterparty survives; margin received against it reduces both the counterparty risk and the funding cost.
explanation: The positive value has a credit dimension (loss on default) and a funding dimension (an asset to be funded). Reusable margin held against it reduces both.
originalText: A positive portfolio value is at risk if the counterparty defaults and is also an asset that must be funded while the counterparty survives; margin received against it reduces both the counterparty risk and the funding cost.

statement: A positive portfolio value creates a funding cost only if the counterparty defaults.
explanation: Funding arises in the scenarios where the counterparty survives. On default the exposure is lost, which is the credit risk.
originalText: A positive portfolio value creates a funding cost only if the counterparty defaults, since funding needs arise from the close-out of the transactions.

statement: A negative derivatives portfolio value creates a funding cost for the bank.
explanation: A negative value is a source of funding and so a funding benefit, not a cost.
originalText: A negative portfolio value creates a funding cost, because the bank must eventually pay the amount it owes to the counterparty.
correction: A negative derivatives portfolio value creates a funding benefit for the bank.

statement: Margin posted by a bank against a negative portfolio value increases the bank's funding benefit.
explanation: Posted margin reduces the bank's funding benefit, because it must give up the funding that the negative value provided.
originalText: Margin posted by the bank against a negative value increases the bank’s funding benefit and reduces the counterparty’s exposure to the bank’s default.
correction: Margin posted by a bank against a negative portfolio value reduces the bank's funding benefit.

statement: Liquid bonds such as gilts can be repoed, so the repo cash largely offsets their funding cost, whereas derivatives cannot be repoed; because funding is assessed at portfolio level, negative-value derivatives provide a funding benefit that offsets part of the cost of positive-value ones.
explanation: Costs and benefits partly cancel because funding needs to be considered only at portfolio level, where values are additive across counterparties.
originalText: The gilts can be repoed, so the repo cash largely offsets their funding cost; the swaps cannot be repoed, but because funding is assessed at portfolio level the negative values provide a benefit that offsets part of the cost of the positive values.

statement: Funding exposure is assessed counterparty by counterparty, like credit exposure, so negative-value swaps with one counterparty provide no funding offset to positive-value swaps with another.
explanation: Netting-set aggregation belongs to credit exposure. Funding applies at portfolio level, where values are additive across counterparties.
originalText: Funding is assessed counterparty by counterparty, like credit exposure, so the negative swaps provide no offset to the positive swaps.

statement: A derivatives portfolio with a negative value creates a funding cost that adds to the funding cost of positive-value portfolios.
explanation: A negative value is a funding benefit that offsets part of the funding cost of positive values.
originalText: The negative swaps create a funding cost equal to their value, which adds to the cost of funding the positive swaps.

statement: Credit exposure is measured netting set by netting set, so a positive value with one counterparty is not offset by a negative value with another without a netting agreement, whereas funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.
explanation: Close-out netting applies only within a netting agreement. For funding, an asset with one counterparty and a liability with another offset, leaving a roughly flat funding position.
originalText: Credit exposure is USD 40 million to X, while the funding position across the two sets is roughly flat, because funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.

statement: Funding, like credit exposure, is assessed netting set by netting set.
explanation: Netting-set aggregation belongs to credit exposure. Funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.
originalText: Credit exposure is USD 40 million to X and the funding requirement is USD 40 million, because funding, like credit exposure, is assessed netting set by netting set.

statement: CVA is measured over a margin period of risk that assumes the counterparty has defaulted and stopped posting margin, leaving residual exposure, whereas funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay, and reusable cash margin offsets the value to be funded.
explanation: This is one reason why a collateralised derivative can have a material CVA but an FVA close to zero.
originalText: CVA is measured over a margin period of risk that assumes the dealer has defaulted and stopped posting, leaving residual exposure; funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay, and the reusable cash margin offsets the value to be funded.

statement: Funding and credit exposure use the same margin period of risk, so the FVA of a collateralised derivative should equal its CVA.
explanation: The two use different periods: CVA uses the margin period of risk, which assumes the counterparty has stopped posting, while funding uses the normal posting frequency. A material CVA with a near-zero FVA is therefore expected.
originalText: The FVA should equal the CVA, because funding and credit exposure use the same margin period of risk; the FVA calculation is therefore in error.

statement: CVA matters to any institution with significant OTC derivatives, including corporates that hedge economic risks, and it became a key topic because of volatile credit spreads and the related accounting and capital requirements.
explanation: GARP names three drivers: credit spread volatility, accounting requirements (IFRS 13) and capital requirements (Basel III). The calculation is a major concern for banks but also for other financial institutions and corporations.
originalText: CVA matters to any institution with significant OTC derivatives, including corporates that hedge economic risks; it became a key topic because of volatile credit spreads and the related accounting and capital requirements.

statement: CVA is relevant only to banks and has no role in a corporate's accounts.
explanation: CVA is a fair-value (accounting) adjustment as well as a capital topic, and it applies to corporations and other institutions with significant OTC derivatives.
originalText: CVA matters only to banks, because it was introduced by Basel III as a regulatory capital charge and has no role in a corporate’s accounts.

statement: Netting and collateral remove counterparty risk entirely, so CVA is relevant only for trades outside a netting agreement.
explanation: Netting and collateral reduce CVA, and must be reflected in it, but they do not remove counterparty risk entirely.
originalText: CVA matters only for trades outside a netting agreement, because netting and collateral remove counterparty risk entirely and leave nothing to price.

statement: CVA needs to be computed only after a counterparty has been downgraded; until then the risk-free value of a derivative is its fair value.
explanation: Default can happen at any time and spreads move continuously, so CVA is part of fair value from the trade date, not something triggered by a downgrade.
originalText: CVA needs to be computed only after a counterparty has been downgraded; until then the risk-free value of the derivative is its fair value.

statement: Most counterparties have no liquid single-name CDS and so need proxy credit spread curves in CVA calculations; the market-implied default probabilities are well above real-world ones and generally cannot be hedged, yet accounting standards still generally require credit spreads.
explanation: GARP lists three objections to market-implied probabilities: they are well above real-world ones, default cannot in general be hedged, and banks warehouse credit risk. In practice the objections are somewhat academic because accounting standards require credit spreads.
originalText: Most counterparties need proxy credit spread curves; the implied default probabilities are well above real-world ones and usually cannot be hedged, yet accounting standards generally still require credit spreads.

statement: For counterparties without liquid CDS, accounting standards require a switch to historical default probabilities, so no proxy curves are needed.
explanation: The standard response to missing CDS is a proxy credit spread curve. Historical default probabilities are used only in rare cases, not by rule.
originalText: For counterparties without liquid CDS, accounting standards require the desk to switch to historical default probabilities, so no proxy curves are needed.

statement: Market-implied default probabilities are generally lower than real-world default probabilities.
explanation: Market-implied default probabilities are significantly higher than real-world ones, so CVA based on credit spreads is larger than the actuarial expected loss.
originalText: Market-implied default probabilities are generally lower than real-world estimates, so CVA based on credit spreads understates the actuarial expected loss.
correction: Market-implied default probabilities are generally higher than real-world default probabilities.

statement: A bank that warehouses credit risk rather than hedging it is exposed only to risk-neutral default risk.
explanation: A bank that warehouses credit risk bears real-world default risk. GARP uses this as an argument against using market-implied default probabilities.
originalText: Because the dealer warehouses its credit risk rather than hedging it, it is exposed only to risk-neutral default risk, which is the main argument for market-implied default probabilities.
correction: A bank that warehouses credit risk rather than hedging it is exposed only to real-world default risk.

statement: Valuing exotic trades inside an exposure simulation may itself need Monte Carlo, so approximations are common (for example, treating a Bermudan swaption as a European one), and path-dependent exposure needs the whole path to each date.
explanation: Nested simulation is expensive, so approximations are used, such as treating a swaption as a forward swap or a Bermudan payoff as a European one. For collateralised netting sets the margin already called depends on the path to each date.
originalText: Valuing exotics inside an exposure simulation may itself need Monte Carlo, so approximations are common (for example, a Bermudan treated as a European), and path-dependent exposure needs the whole path to each date.

statement: Exotic and path-dependent trades affect only the counterparty's default probability and leave the exposure model unchanged.
explanation: Exotic trades and collateral change the exposure profile, not the counterparty's default probability, so the exposure model must handle them.
originalText: Exotic and path-dependent trades change only the counterparty’s default probability, so the team should recalibrate the credit curve and leave the exposure model unchanged.

statement: Margin removes the exposure on collateralised netting sets entirely, so they can be dropped from the CVA calculation.
explanation: Margin reduces CVA but does not remove it, because the margin period of risk leaves residual exposure.
originalText: Collateralised netting sets can be dropped from the CVA calculation because margin removes the exposure, so only the Bermudan swaptions need to be simulated.

statement: CVA is the difference between the value of a derivatives portfolio with and without counterparty default; in Gregory's convention it is negative, so the risky value equals the risk-free value plus CVA.
explanation: Either way the risky value is below the risk-free value. Some sources quote CVA as a positive cost and subtract it.
originalText: CVA is the difference between the value of a derivatives portfolio with and without counterparty default; in Gregory’s convention it is negative, so the risky value is the risk-free value plus CVA.

statement: CVA is the 99th percentile loss from counterparty default over one year, held as capital against a derivatives portfolio.
explanation: A 99th percentile loss is a capital or risk measure. CVA is an expected value, a price.
originalText: CVA is the 99th percentile loss from counterparty default over one year, held as capital against the derivatives portfolio.

statement: CVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.
explanation: That describes DVA. CVA is based on the expected positive exposure to the counterparty and the counterparty's default probability.
originalText: CVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.
correction: DVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.

statement: CVA is the sum of the standalone adjustments of each trade with the counterparty, so it is unaffected by netting and collateral agreements.
explanation: Netting and collateral reduce the CVA of a netting set, so it is not the sum of standalone trade adjustments.
originalText: CVA is the sum of the standalone adjustments of each trade with the counterparty, so it is unaffected by netting and collateral agreements.

statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities, with a single average LGD, assumes that default time, exposure at default and LGD are independent, that is, no wrong-way risk.
explanation: If the three components are independent, the expectation of their product splits into the product of expectations: a single average LGD, the unconditional EPE at each date and the marginal default probability.
originalText: It assumes default time, exposure at default and LGD are independent (no wrong-way risk), which lets the expectation split into EPE times marginal PD with one average LGD.

statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities assumes a constant hazard rate, so it cannot be used when the credit curve is upward sloping or inverted.
explanation: The marginal default probabilities can come from any credit curve shape; a constant hazard rate is a convenience, not an assumption of the formula.
originalText: It assumes the counterparty’s hazard rate is constant, so it cannot be used when the credit curve is upward sloping or inverted.

statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities assumes that exposure and default are positively dependent, so each EPE is measured conditional on the counterparty defaulting at that date.
explanation: That describes the wrong-way risk extension with conditional EPE. The simple form leaves wrong-way risk out by assuming independence.
originalText: It assumes exposure and default are positively dependent, so each EPE is measured conditional on the counterparty defaulting at that date.

statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities assumes that LGD is zero on collateralised trades, so only uncollateralised netting sets enter the sum.
explanation: Collateral reduces the EPE; it does not set LGD to zero or remove netting sets from the CVA calculation.
originalText: It assumes the LGD is zero on collateralised trades, so only uncollateralised netting sets need to enter the sum.

statement: When a position is very deep in the money, its EPE can be approximated by its expected future value, so the CVA calculation converges to a simpler, bond-like discounting calculation.
explanation: EPE averages $\max(V, 0)$. If $V$ is almost never negative, $\max(V, 0) \approx V$, so EPE is close to the expected future value; the discounting approach must still allow for LGD.
originalText: When a position is very in the money, its EPE can be approximated by its expected future value, so the CVA calculation converges to a simpler, bond-like discounting calculation.

statement: The CVA of a deeply in-the-money position should be based on potential future exposure at a high percentile rather than on expected positive exposure.
explanation: CVA always uses the expected exposure; PFE is a limit-setting measure whatever the moneyness of the position.
originalText: Because the swap is deeply in the money, CVA should be based on its potential future exposure at a high percentile rather than on its EPE.

statement: For a deeply in-the-money position, CVA no longer depends on the loss given default.
explanation: LGD still scales the loss. Dropping it would treat the entire exposure as lost on default.
originalText: Because the exposure is almost certain to stay positive, CVA no longer depends on the loss given default and equals the expected future value times the cumulative default probability.

statement: The netting benefit in CVA is large when the trades in a netting set offset each other and small when they are all in the same direction: same-direction trades give a netting-set EPE close to the sum of standalone EPEs, while offsetting trades make it far lower.
explanation: Aggregation reduces exposure only in scenarios where trade values have opposite signs. Trades in the same direction rarely have opposite signs.
originalText: The netting benefit is large for Y and small for X: X’s netting-set CVA is close to the sum of its standalone CVAs, while Y’s offsetting trades make its netting-set EPE far lower than the sum of standalone EPEs.

statement: The netting benefit in CVA depends only on the number of trades in the netting set.
explanation: The benefit depends on the correlation, or sign pattern, of the trade values and not on the number of trades.
originalText: The netting benefit is the same for both, because it depends only on the number of trades in the netting set.

statement: The netting benefit in CVA is larger when the trades in the netting set are all in the same direction.
explanation: Same-direction trades reinforce each other and offset least, so netting has little to cancel; the benefit is larger when trades offset.
originalText: The netting benefit is larger for X, because trades in the same direction reinforce each other’s exposure and netting removes this concentration.
correction: The netting benefit in CVA is larger when the trades in the netting set are in offsetting directions.

statement: Netting lowers the counterparty's probability of default, which is why it reduces CVA.
explanation: Netting acts on the exposure, path by path, and leaves the default probability unchanged.
originalText: The netting benefit is larger for Y, because netting lowers Y’s default probability, which depends on its offsetting positions.

statement: To incorporate netting into CVA, EPE is computed separately for each legally enforceable netting set by netting trade values before taking the positive part; trades without an enforceable netting agreement are each treated as their own netting set; the netting-set CVAs are then added, using the same PD and LGD.
explanation: A netting set is the group of trades under one legally enforceable netting agreement, and there may be more than one with a counterparty. Where netting is not enforceable, each trade's gross positive exposure counts.
originalText: Compute EPE separately for each enforceable netting set, netting trade values before taking the positive part; treat each trade in group (3) as its own netting set; then add the CVAs, using the same PD and LGD throughout.

statement: All trades with a counterparty can be netted into a single exposure for CVA because CVA depends on the counterparty's single default probability.
explanation: Netting is a legal right within an enforceable agreement, not a consequence of the counterparty having one default probability.
originalText: Net all the trades with the counterparty into a single exposure, because CVA depends on the counterparty’s one default probability.

statement: When the two parties have equal credit spreads and LGDs, BCVA without survival adjustments depends on EPE plus ENE, which equals the expected future value; because that is additive across trades, the CVA and DVA effects of netting offset and there is no incremental netting benefit.
explanation: With equal marginal default probabilities the BCVA is proportional to $\text{EPE} + \text{ENE} = \text{EFV}$, and the EFV is additive across trades.
originalText: The trader is wrong: with equal spreads and LGDs, BCVA depends on EPE plus ENE, which is the expected future value; that is additive across trades, so the CVA and DVA effects of netting offset and there is no incremental netting benefit.

statement: Adding an offsetting swap to a netting set reduces the CVA leg of BCVA while leaving the DVA leg unaffected.
explanation: The offset shrinks the expected negative exposure as well, so the DVA leg falls too.
originalText: The trader is right: the offsetting swap lowers the netting set’s EPE, so the CVA leg shrinks while the DVA leg is unaffected, giving a large BCVA benefit.

statement: Netting increases the size of both the EPE and the ENE of a netting set.
explanation: Netting reduces the size of both the expected positive exposure and the expected negative exposure.
originalText: The trader is wrong: netting raises both EPE and ENE in size, so the new swap makes BCVA more negative.
correction: Netting reduces the size of both the EPE and the ENE of a netting set.

statement: Netting lowers the DVA leg of BCVA but leaves the CVA leg unchanged.
explanation: Netting reduces both the CVA leg and the DVA leg, not only the DVA leg.
originalText: The trader is right: netting lowers the DVA leg but leaves the CVA leg unchanged, so BCVA becomes less negative.

statement: Margin mitigates wrong-way risk at a CCP only if exposure builds gradually before a default; jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk can exhaust initial margin, and the margin-posting members are mostly systemic banks whose defaults bring the most extreme wrong-way risk.
explanation: If exposure increases gradually before default, margin can be received; a jump in exposure makes margin useless. Initial margin set at normal coverage can be exhausted in a stressed close-out.
originalText: Disagree: margin mitigates WWR only if exposure builds gradually before a default; jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk can exhaust initial margin, and the members that post margin are mostly systemic banks whose defaults bring the most extreme WWR.

statement: Margin removes wrong-way risk at a CCP, because variation margin is received continuously as the exposure to a member rises.
explanation: Margin arrives with a lag and cannot keep up with a jump in exposure at default, so it mitigates wrong-way risk but does not remove it.
originalText: Agree: margin removes WWR at a CCP, because variation margin is received continuously as the exposure to a member rises.

statement: Wrong-way risk matters only for uncollateralised counterparties such as corporates, not for margin-posting clearing members.
explanation: The members that actively post margin are mainly banks, which are highly systemic and face the most extreme wrong-way risk.
originalText: Agree: WWR matters only for uncollateralised counterparties such as corporates, and corporates are not clearing members.

statement: Margin posted by a clearing member increases wrong-way risk because it always loses its value when that member defaults.
explanation: Only specific collateral, such as a member's own bonds, is linked to its default. Margin in general still reduces exposure.
originalText: Disagree: margin increases WWR, because collateral posted by a member always loses its value when that member defaults.

statement: Ideally cleared products carry no wrong-way risk, but a clearing member's default can be adversely linked to the value of the CDSs it has traded, so values can move sharply just as it defaults, complicating default management and the wrong-way risk part of margin and default funds.
explanation: A member that has sold protection on names correlated with itself, such as other financials or its sovereign, owes much more exactly when it defaults. This is why single-name CDSs are hard to clear.
originalText: Ideally cleared products carry no WWR, but a member’s default can be adversely linked to the value of the CDSs it has traded (for example, protection sold on correlated financials), so values can move sharply just as it defaults, complicating default management and the WWR part of margin and default funds.

statement: Because CDSs are illiquid by construction, a CCP cannot compute variation margin on them at all.
explanation: Liquidity is a clearability criterion, but CDSs are cleared with variation margin; illiquidity is not the reason they are hard to clear.
originalText: CDSs are illiquid by construction, so a CCP cannot compute variation margin on them at all.

statement: Once CDSs are cleared they carry no wrong-way risk, because multilateral netting offsets protection bought and sold across members.
explanation: Netting offsets market risk across members, but the CCP still faces each member's default, so wrong-way risk remains.
originalText: Once cleared, CDSs carry no WWR, because multilateral netting offsets protection bought and sold across members, so the diﬀiculty is purely operational.

statement: Central clearing does not eliminate wrong-way risk: a CCP's book is matched only while all members perform, a member's default leaves it unmatched just when wrong-way risk bites, and losses beyond the defaulter's resources and the CCP's equity fall on surviving members.
explanation: The CCP has conditional market risk: after a member default it has an unmatched book to hedge and auction, and the defaulter's positions move sharply against it at that moment. Defaulter-pays resources come first, and any excess loss is mutualised.
originalText: Disagree: the book is matched only while all members perform; a default leaves it unmatched just when WWR bites, and losses beyond the defaulter’s resources and CCP equity fall on surviving members.

statement: After novation a CCP has no net market risk in any circumstances, so a member's default cannot produce wrong-way losses for anyone.
explanation: The book is matched only while every member performs. A default leaves the CCP with an unmatched book, which is exactly when wrong-way risk matters.
originalText: Agree: after novation the CCP has no net market risk in any circumstances, so a member’s default cannot produce wrong-way losses for anyone.

statement: Initial margin is designed to cover every possible close-out loss on a defaulting clearing member's positions.
explanation: Initial margin is set to a confidence level, not to cover every loss, so the defaulter-pays resources may prove insufficient under wrong-way risk.
originalText: Agree: the wrong-way risk now sits entirely in the defaulting member’s own initial margin, which by design covers every possible close-out loss.

statement: Clearing increases wrong-way risk mainly because the CCP must post initial margin to its members, which it loses when a member defaults.
explanation: Members post initial margin to the CCP, not the reverse. The risk comes from the defaulter's positions and the mutualised default fund.
originalText: Disagree: clearing increases wrong-way risk mainly because the CCP must post initial margin to its members, which it loses when a member defaults.

statement: For the minimum capital requirement, expected positive exposure is the time-weighted average of the expected exposures over the first year, each weighted by the share of the year that its interval represents.
explanation: With reporting dates at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months the intervals are unequal (1, 2, 3 and 6 months), so weights of 1/12, 2/12, 3/12 and 6/12 apply rather than equal weights.
originalText: The time-weighted average of the expected exposures over the first year, each weighted by the share of the year that its interval represents.

statement: For the minimum capital requirement, expected positive exposure is the simple average of all the expected exposures over the life of the netting set, with each reporting date counted once.
explanation: The capital EPE is taken over the first year, and unequal reporting intervals need time weights, not equal weights.
originalText: The simple average of all the expected exposures out to year 7, with each reporting date counted once.

statement: Expected positive exposure is the highest 95th-percentile exposure reported over the first year.
explanation: That describes a maximum peak exposure, a tail statistic. EPE is a weighted average of expected exposures.
originalText: The highest 95th-percentile exposure reported over the first year.

statement: For the minimum capital requirement, expected positive exposure is the expected exposure at the one-year date.
explanation: The one-year expected exposure is a single point of the expected exposure profile. EPE is the time-weighted average of the profile.
originalText: The expected exposure at the one-year date, since capital is held for one year.

statement: When counterparty credit risk is viewed as a credit risk, its measures are current exposure, peak exposure and expected exposure; when it is viewed as a market risk, they are CVA and the variability of CVA, for example the VaR of CVA.
explanation: Exposures belong to the credit view, while CVA and its changes belong to the market view.
originalText: Credit-risk view: current exposure, peak exposure and expected exposure; market-risk view: CVA and the variability of CVA, for example the VaR of CVA.

statement: CVA and peak exposure are measures of counterparty credit risk viewed as a credit risk, while current exposure and expected exposure belong to the market-risk view.
explanation: CVA is the market view's measure, whereas current, peak and expected exposure are all credit-view measures.
originalText: Credit-risk view: CVA and peak exposure; market-risk view: current exposure and expected exposure.

statement: A bank that treats counterparty credit risk purely as a credit risk can still be exposed to changes in CVA as credit spreads and exposures move, which can produce balance-sheet surprises unless CVA is included in the valuation of its derivatives.
explanation: Limits, collateral and netting manage the default side of CCR. They do not capture changes in the fair value of counterparty risk.
originalText: Changes in the market value of counterparty risk (CVA) as credit spreads and exposures move, which can produce balance-sheet surprises.

statement: Collateral and netting remove every source of counterparty risk except wrong-way risk.
explanation: Collateral and netting do not remove CVA risk, and wrong-way risk is not the only residual risk.
originalText: Wrong-way risk only, since collateral and netting remove every other source of counterparty risk.

statement: Limits, collateral and netting together capture all counterparty risk in a derivatives portfolio.
explanation: Adopting the credit view alone leaves a bank blind to the market view, including changes in CVA.
originalText: None of significance, since limits, collateral and netting together capture all counterparty risk in a derivatives portfolio.

statement: A dealer that treats counterparty risk as a credit risk must replace all of a defaulting counterparty's trades in the market at once at default, whereas a dealer that treats it as a market risk and manages CVA dynamically has already moved trades to other counterparties in proportion to the rising probability of default.
explanation: For the market-view dealer the default is therefore close to a non-event.
originalText: K must replace all of the defaulting counterparty’s trades in the market at once at default; M has already moved trades to other counterparties in proportion to the rising probability of default, so the default is close to a non-event for M.

statement: A dealer that treats counterparty risk as a credit risk replaces the counterparty's trades gradually, in proportion to its probability of default, so the default is a non-event for it.
explanation: That describes the market-risk view. The credit-view dealer must replace all the trades at once at default.
originalText: K replaces the counterparty’s trades gradually, in proportion to its probability of default, so the default is a non-event for K; M must replace all the trades at once at default.

statement: Under both the credit-risk and the market-risk view of counterparty risk, it can be managed only at inception and not before default.
explanation: This is true only of the credit view. The market view acts before default by moving trades as the probability of default rises.
originalText: Neither dealer can act before default, because under both views counterparty risk can be managed only at inception.

statement: Treating counterparty credit risk as a credit risk was the predominant framework from 2000 to 2006 and the basis of Basel II capital, while the market-risk treatment was largely confined to pricing CVA until the 2007-08 financial crisis.
explanation: Potential exposure and EPE models are the hallmark of the credit view, which was established as the basis for regulatory capital under Basel II.
originalText: Treating CCR as a credit risk was the predominant framework from 2000 to 2006 and the basis of Basel II capital, while the market-risk treatment was largely confined to pricing CVA until the 2007-08 crisis.

statement: Stress testing of counterparty credit risk evolved faster than the statistical measures of counterparty credit risk.
explanation: Statistical measures of CCR progressed faster than stress testing.
originalText: Stress testing of CCR evolved faster than the statistical measures of CCR, which is why the chapter builds the statistical measures on top of stress tests.
correction: Stress testing of counterparty credit risk evolved more slowly than the statistical measures of counterparty credit risk.

statement: Before the 2007-08 financial crisis, CVA was a large and volatile part of bank derivative valuations.
explanation: Before the crisis credit spreads were stable and CVA was a small part of valuations.
originalText: Before the crisis CVA was a large and volatile part of bank derivative valuations, which prompted the FAS 157 accounting requirement.

statement: During the 2007-08 crisis, swings in credit spreads and exposures produced large CVA losses but no gains.
explanation: The crisis produced both large losses and large, unusual gains on CVA, because spreads and exposures moved in both directions.
originalText: During the crisis the combined swings in credit spreads and exposures produced large CVA losses but no gains, since credit spreads only widened.

statement: A table of stressed current exposures shows which counterparties would owe the bank most in a scenario, but it cannot say which counterparty is the greater concern, because stressed current exposure ignores credit quality.
explanation: Stressed current exposure ranks exposure, not loss, and omits each counterparty's willingness or ability to pay.
originalText: The table shows which counterparties would owe the bank most if equities fell 25%, but it cannot say whether C or D is the greater concern, because stressed current exposure ignores credit quality.

statement: The sum of the stressed current exposures across counterparties is the loss the bank would suffer in the stress scenario.
explanation: The sum would be the loss only if every counterparty defaulted in the scenario.
originalText: The equity crash would cost the bank about US\$539 million, the sum of the stressed current exposures.

statement: A counterparty with a larger stressed current exposure is necessarily a greater concern than one with a smaller exposure, whatever their credit quality.
explanation: Stressed current exposure ignores credit quality, so a larger exposure to a strong counterparty need not be the greater concern than a smaller exposure to a weak one.
originalText: Counterparty C is a greater concern than counterparty D in this scenario, because its stressed current exposure is larger.

statement: A counterparty whose trades are fully collateralised today needs no further attention in a stress scenario.
explanation: The stressed exposure is measured before any further collateral is collected, so a fully collateralised counterparty can still show a large stressed exposure.
originalText: Counterparty D needs no further attention in this scenario, because its trades are fully collateralised today.

statement: In the expected-loss stress test of a loan portfolio, EAD and LGD are held fixed, each PD is modelled as a function of variables such as the unemployment rate or an important exchange rate, those variables are set to stressed values, and expected loss is recomputed with the stressed PDs.
explanation: The stress loss is the stressed expected loss minus the base expected loss, where expected loss is the sum of PD times EAD times LGD across the pool.
originalText: Hold EAD and LGD fixed, model each PD as a function of variables such as the unemployment rate or an important exchange rate, set those variables to stressed values, and recompute expected loss with the stressed PDs.

statement: The stress test of a loan portfolio holds PDs fixed and stresses each EAD through instantaneous shocks to equity prices and swap rates.
explanation: Loan exposures are insensitive to market variables; the loan stress works through the probability of default.
originalText: Hold the PDs fixed and stress each EAD through instantaneous shocks to equity prices and swap rates, since the loans’ exposures move with market variables.

statement: In the stress test of a loan portfolio, each EAD is replaced with alpha times EPE.
explanation: Alpha times EPE replaces EAD only for derivatives, whose exposure is stochastic. For loans, EAD is taken as deterministic.
originalText: Replace each EAD with alpha times EPE, and stress EPE by re-running the exposure simulation after a market shock.

statement: An instantaneous market shock applied in a CVA stress test changes today's market values, so the expected exposures in all later periods must be recalculated, and the marginal default probabilities are restated from the shocked credit spread.
explanation: Stresses to the marginal probability of default are usually derived from credit spread shocks.
originalText: The shock changes today’s market values, so the expected exposures in all later periods must be recalculated, and the marginal default probabilities are restated from the shocked credit spread.

statement: In a CVA stress test, an instantaneous shock changes only the expected exposure in the first time bucket, while later buckets keep their base values.
explanation: The shock is applied today but affects every later expected exposure, so the whole expected exposure profile has to be recalculated.
originalText: Only the expected exposure in the first time bucket changes, because the shock is instantaneous; later buckets keep their base values.

statement: In a CVA stress test the expected exposures are left unchanged and only LGD is stressed.
explanation: The scenario's main effects are on the exposures and the default probabilities; LGD can also be stressed, but not alone.
originalText: The expected exposures are left unchanged and only the LGD is stressed, since CVA is linear in LGD.

statement: Replacing each period's expected exposure with the stressed current exposure gives the same stressed CVA at lower cost.
explanation: Current exposure is not a substitute for expected exposure; using it is a common pitfall in stress testing CCR.
originalText: The desk replaces each period’s expected exposure with the stressed current exposure, which gives the same answer at lower cost.

statement: A CVA stress uses risk-neutral values, losses over the life of the transactions and a market-based model of default probability, whereas the expected-loss stress of counterparty credit risk uses physical values over a specified horizon.
explanation: Both stresses rely on expected loss being the product of LGD, exposure and probability of default, but the inputs differ.
originalText: The CVA stress uses risk-neutral values, losses over the life of the transactions and a market-based model of default probability, while the expected-loss stress uses physical values over a specified horizon.

statement: The CVA stress and the expected-loss stress of counterparty credit risk both use physical default probabilities over a one-year horizon and differ only in the exposure measure.
explanation: The CVA stress uses risk-neutral default probabilities over the life of the trades, so the two differ in more than the exposure measure.
originalText: Both use physical default probabilities over a one-year horizon; they differ only in the exposure measure.
