statement: The expected-loss stress of counterparty credit risk uses default probabilities implied from CDS spreads, while the CVA stress uses historical default rates.
explanation: This swaps the two views: spread-implied probabilities belong to the CVA stress, and the expected-loss stress uses physical probabilities.
originalText: The expected-loss stress uses default probabilities implied from CDS spreads, while the CVA stress uses historical default rates.

statement: The CVA stress and the expected-loss stress give the same stress loss for the same scenario, because both are products of LGD, exposure and default probability.
explanation: The two share a structure but use different inputs, so their values will be quite different.
originalText: Because both are products of LGD, exposure and default probability, the two exercises give the same stress loss for the same scenario.

statement: When CVA is computed with market-implied default probabilities and a model that correlates exposure with default probability, a recommended additional stress test is to stress that correlation, to see the profit-and-loss impact if the correlation is wrong.
explanation: Since the correlation is highly uncertain, institutions should run stress tests to see the impact if it is wrong (Hull and White, 2012).
originalText: A stress of the correlation between exposure and the default probability, to see the profit-and-loss impact if the correlation is wrong.

statement: The DVA term of bilateral CVA captures wrong-way risk.
explanation: DVA reflects the bank's own default and does not capture wrong-way risk. Wrong-way risk comes from the correlation between exposure and the counterparty's default probability.
originalText: A stress of the bank’s own default probability, since the DVA term captures wrong-way risk.

statement: For a linear derivative with no intermediate payments, the error from using the change in stressed current exposure in place of the change in expected exposure is largest when the position is close to at the money.
explanation: Current exposure is a hinge at zero, so its change jumps from 0 to the full shock over a narrow band, whereas expected exposure averages over future scenarios and moves smoothly.
originalText: Close to at the money, where the difference between the two changes is almost half the value of the shock.

statement: The error from using stressed current exposure in place of expected exposure is largest for a position that is deep in the money.
explanation: Deep in the money both exposures rise by almost the full shock, so the gap is small.
originalText: Deep in the money, because current exposure then takes the full shock while expected exposure takes almost none of it.

statement: The error from using stressed current exposure in place of expected exposure is largest for a position that is deep out of the money.
explanation: Deep out of the money both exposures barely move, so the gap is small.
originalText: Deep out of the money, because current exposure stays at zero while expected exposure takes almost all of the shock.

statement: More integrated CCR stress tests come from combining the credit-risk view of CCR with the loan portfolio and the market-risk view with the trading book, but combining default stresses and fair-value stresses into one comprehensive test remains the true difficulty.
explanation: The two integrations are the end points of the credit and market views; the remaining difficulty is producing a single comprehensive stress test.
originalText: More integrated stress tests come from combining the credit-risk view of CCR with the loan portfolio and the market-risk view with the trading book, but combining default stresses and fair-value stresses into one comprehensive test remains the true diﬀiculty.

statement: The more CCR stress tests a bank runs, the clearer its view of the risk, so the programme should report every available stress result.
explanation: Too many stress tests can hide the risk of a portfolio; a fair number is needed, not every possible result.
originalText: The more CCR stress tests the bank runs, the clearer its view of the risk, so the programme should report every available stress result.

statement: A bank that manages counterparty credit risk purely as a credit risk avoids fair-value losses, so it needs to stress only default losses.
explanation: Fair value losses and default losses can occur no matter how a financial institution manages its CCR.
originalText: A bank that manages CCR purely as a credit risk avoids fair-value losses, so it needs to stress only default losses.

statement: Central clearing has removed the need for CCR stress testing.
explanation: Regulators moved derivatives to central clearing just as CCR management was advancing; clearing does not make stress testing unnecessary.
originalText: Central clearing has removed the need for CCR stress testing, which is why the chapter describes the recent advances in CCR management as ironic.

statement: Running PD and market stresses through expected positive exposure scaled by alpha in the expected-loss framework allows derivative stress losses to be added to loan stress losses.
explanation: Alpha times EPE allows CCR exposures to be placed in a portfolio credit model along with loans, so both are measured in the same units on the same physical-PD basis.
originalText: Run the PD and market stresses through expected positive exposure scaled by alpha in the expected-loss framework, so that derivative stress losses can be added to the loan stress losses.

statement: The sum of the stressed current exposures across all counterparties in a scenario is the stress loss of the derivatives book and can be compared with the stress loss of the loan book.
explanation: The sum would be the loss only if every counterparty defaulted, and current exposure ignores credit quality, so it cannot be compared with an expected-loss stress on loans.
originalText: Sum the stressed current exposures across all counterparties in each scenario and report that total as the stress loss of the derivatives book for comparison with the loan book.

statement: Delta approximations for repricing derivatives under large scenario shocks are most reliable for portfolios close to at the money.
explanation: CCR is highly nonlinear, and at-the-money portfolios with large price moves are especially prone to errors from delta approximations.
originalText: Reprice the derivatives under the large scenario shocks using delta sensitivities, since the linear approximation is most reliable for portfolios that are close to at-the-money.
correction: Delta approximations for repricing derivatives under large scenario shocks are least reliable for portfolios close to at the money.

statement: Including DVA in a CVA stress test can only reduce reported stress losses and never creates a loss from changes in the bank's own credit quality.
explanation: The bilateral formula can produce counterintuitive results, such as losses when the firm's own credit quality improves; the liability side should be included to capture the full impact on CVA profit and loss.
originalText: Leave DVA out of the CVA stress test, since a bilateral view can only reduce reported stress losses and never creates a loss from changes in the bank’s own credit quality.

statement: A Gaussian copula correlation calibrated to market tranche prices is an implied credit correlation with no direct economic interpretation, although it equals the correlation of a Gaussian single-factor model.
explanation: Copula correlations are the values entered in the off-diagonal cells of the copula's correlation matrix. The implied credit correlation is an estimate of the copula correlation derived from market prices.
originalText: The parameter is a copula correlation inferred from prices; it has no direct economic interpretation, but it equals the correlation of a Gaussian single-factor model.

statement: A copula correlation calibrated to market tranche prices is the constituents' default correlation, the correlation of their default indicators.
explanation: Default correlation, the correlation of default indicators, is a different concept and is not what the calibration produces.
originalText: The parameter is the constituents’ default correlation, the correlation of their default indicators, so it can be checked against historical joint default frequencies.

statement: A copula correlation calibrated to market tranche prices is the constituents' asset return correlation, which can be measured directly as the correlation of their equity returns.
explanation: Asset return correlation drives Merton-type models and is only proxied by equity correlation; neither is the calibrated copula parameter.
originalText: The parameter is the constituents’ asset return correlation, so it can be measured directly as the correlation of their equity returns.

statement: A copula correlation calibrated to the observed prices of traded tranches is a physical, real-world correlation.
explanation: A parameter calibrated to traded prices, with CDS-implied default probabilities, is risk-neutral rather than physical.
originalText: The parameter is a physical (real-world) correlation, because it is estimated from the observed prices of liquid traded tranches.

statement: A standard credit index tranche has a partial spread01 to each constituent of the index, and moves in spreads or in implied correlation cause mark-to-market changes, whereas in a cash CLO changes in default rates and correlation alter fundamental value.
explanation: A standard tranche has risk-neutral partial spread01s rather than a default01, and each spread01 is itself a function of the implied correlation, which varies in its own right.
originalText: A standard tranche has a partial spread01 to each of the 125 constituents, and moves in spreads or in implied correlation cause mark-to-market changes; in a cash CLO, default rate and correlation changes alter fundamental value.

statement: A standard credit index tranche is valued with physical default probabilities taken from the constituents' ratings, so its main sensitivity is a default01.
explanation: Standard tranches are valued with risk-neutral default probabilities from CDS spreads, and their sensitivities are partial spread01s. The default01 is the cash CLO's measure.
originalText: A standard tranche is valued with physical default probabilities taken from the constituents’ ratings, so its main sensitivity is a default01, measured by shocking those probabilities by 10 bp.

statement: Implied correlation is a pure credit-risk parameter that is fixed when a standard tranche is first traded, so it causes no mark-to-market changes.
explanation: Implied correlation moves with tranche prices and is a market concept, so changes in it are mark-to-market changes.
originalText: Implied correlation is a pure credit-risk parameter that is fixed when a standard tranche is first traded, so it causes no mark-to-market changes in the desk’s positions.

statement: The CDX spread premium is reset every day to the fair spread of the constituents, so standard tranche positions carry no exposure to changes in constituent spreads.
explanation: The CDX spread premium is fixed on the initiation date, so later trading exchanges a present value that moves with the constituent spreads.
originalText: The CDX spread premium is reset every day to the fair spread of the constituents, so standard tranche positions carry no exposure to changes in constituent spreads.

statement: Implied correlation is estimated from rating-based physical default probabilities, so it is a credit risk parameter rather than a market risk parameter.
explanation: Implied correlation is computed from risk-neutral default probabilities taken from single-name CDS spreads. Malz calls it as much a market-risk as a credit-risk concept.
originalText: The implied correlation has risen from 0.30 to 0.60, and because it is estimated from rating-based physical default probabilities, it is a credit risk rather than a market risk parameter.

statement: A mezzanine tranche behaves like an equity tranche at any default rate.
explanation: The mezzanine tranche behaves like the equity tranche only at high default rates; at moderate default rates its expected writedown rises with correlation, unlike the equity.
originalText: The implied correlation has risen from 0.30 to 0.60, and the mezzanine bond’s expected writedown has fallen, because the mezzanine tranche behaves like the equity tranche at any default rate.
